'''Quasi-identifiers''' are pieces of information that are not of themselves [[unique identifier]]s, but are sufficiently well correlated with an entity that they can be combined with other quasi-identifiers to create a unique identifier.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stats.oecd.org/glossary/detail.asp?ID=6961|title=Glossary of Statistical Terms: Quasi-identifier|publisher=OECD|date=November 10, 2005|access-date=29 September 2013|archive-date=7 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131107232557/http://stats.oecd.org/glossary/detail.asp?ID=6961|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Quasi-identifiers can thus, when combined, become [[personally identifying information]]. This process is called [[re-identification]]. As an example, [[Latanya Sweeney]] has shown that even though neither [[gender]], [[birth date]]s nor [[postal code]]s uniquely identify an individual, the combination of all three is sufficient to identify 87% of individuals in the United States.<ref>Sweeney, Latanya. ''Simple demographics often identify people uniquely''. Carnegie Mellon University, 2000. https://dataprivacylab.org/projects/identifiability/paper1.pdf</ref> 

The term was introduced by Tore Dalenius in 1986.<ref>Dalenius, Tore. ''Finding a Needle In a Haystack or Identifying Anonymous Census Records''. Journal of Official Statistics, Vol.2, No.3, 1986.  pp. 329–336. http://www.jos.nu/Articles/abstract.asp?article=23329 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808033912/http://www.jos.nu/Articles/abstract.asp?article=23329 |date=2017-08-08 }}</ref> Since then, quasi-identifiers have been the basis of several attacks on released data. For instance, Sweeney linked health records to publicly available information to locate the then-governor of Massachusetts' hospital records using uniquely identifying quasi-identifiers,<ref>Anderson, Nate. 
''Anonymized'' data really isn’t—and here’s why not. Ars Technica, 2009. https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2009/09/your-secrets-live-online-in-databases-of-ruin/ </ref><ref>Barth-Jones, Daniel C. ''The're-identification'of Governor William Weld's medical information: a critical re-examination of health data identification risks and privacy protections, then and now.'' Then and Now (June 4, 2012) (2012). </ref> and Sweeney, Abu and Winn used public voter records to re-identify participants in the Personal Genome Project.<ref> Sweeney, Latanya, Akua Abu, and Julia Winn. "Identifying participants in the personal genome project by name." Available at SSRN 2257732 (2013).</ref> Additionally, Arvind Narayanan and [[Vitaly Shmatikov]] discussed on quasi-identifiers to indicate statistical conditions for de-anonymizing data released by Netflix.<ref>Narayanan, Arvind and Shmatikov, Vitaly. ''Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets''. The University of Texas at Austin, 2008. https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~shmat/shmat_oak08netflix.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210126130536/https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~shmat/shmat_oak08netflix.pdf |date=2021-01-26 }}</ref>

Motwani and Ying warn about potential privacy breaches being enabled by publication of large volumes of government and business data containing quasi-identifiers.<ref>{{cite conference |title=Efficient Algorithms for Masking and Finding Quasi-Identifiers |author=Rajeev Motwani and Ying Xu |conference=Proceedings of SDM’08 International Workshop on Practical Privacy-Preserving Data Mining |url=https://www.csee.umbc.edu/~kunliu1/p3dm08/proceedings/2.pdf |year=2008}}</ref>
